query: Consider the following context: The recent trend of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) was studied extensively for their promising mechanical properties, but individual constituents' effects have remained unexplored. In that context, which method can be used for the effects of changing the percentage of elements of HfNbTaTiZr-HEA on the mechanical properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using a combinatorial powder metallurgy approach to systematically vary the relative percentages of the five elements in an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy will tune its mechanical properties – specifically, increasing the percentage of Hf relative to elements such as Ti will increase lattice distortion and hinder dislocation movement, thus improving hardness but potentially reducing ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr HEA produced from blended elemental powders.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of individual elemental percentages (e.g., increasing Hf while correspondingly decreasing Ti) using a combinatorial synthesis method (e.g., powder metallurgy with spark plasma sintering) to create an alloy library.
generation.conditions: All samples processed under identical thermal and mechanical processing conditions (e.g., same sintering temperature, pressure, and atmosphere) and tested at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Microstructural changes including increased lattice distortion and possible changes in phase stability that affect dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Higher Hf content leads to increased lattice distortion due to its larger atomic size, which increases hindrance to dislocation slip and thus enhances hardness; however, the trade‐off may be a reduction in ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: A trend in which samples with a higher Hf fraction exhibit higher hardness and yield strength but lower ductility compared to the baseline equiatomic alloy.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr HEA with known mechanical properties prepared via a standard powder metallurgy route.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold under similar processing parameters and at room temperature; deviations may occur if secondary phase formation or processing-induced defects dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative relationship between elemental adjustments and the magnitude of changes in mechanical properties is uncertain due to possible complex interactions among multiple elements and processing sensitivity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HfNbTaTiZr-based alloys where only the Hf/Ti ratio is systematically varied (e.g., by increasing Hf from 20% to 30% while decreasing Ti from 20% to 10% and adjusting other constituents to maintain total mass balance) using the same powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering parameters. Conduct mechanical tests (e.g., hardness and tensile tests) and microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/TEM) on each composition.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Grain size and phase distribution via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanical properties (e.g., hardness and yield strength) do not vary in a consistent trend with changes in the Hf/Ti ratio – or if increasing Hf does not lead to the predicted increase in hardness and corresponding decrease in ductility – then the hypothesis that tuning elemental percentages systematically tailors the mechanical properties via lattice distortion effects would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloys (HEA) have been one of the most attractive groups of materials for researchers in the last several years. Since HEAs are potential candidates for many (e.g., refractory, cryogenic, medical) applications, their properties are studied intensively. The most frequent method of HEA synthesis is arc or induction melting. Powder metallurgy is a perspective technique of alloy synthesis and therefore in this work the possibilities of synthesis of HfNbTaTiZr HEA from powders were studied. Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen. The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content. The microstructure of HfNbTaTiZr specimen prepared this way can be refined by high pressure torsion deformation resulting in a high hardness of 410 HV10 and very fine microstructure with grain size well below 5

High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ].
